newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea opens special probe into banks over Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea opens special probe into banks over Hanbo.

text.p: South Korean authorities on Wednesday opened a special probe into main creditor banks of the debt-striken Hanbo Group and grilled the conglomerate's top executives over a loan scandal.

The state banking watchdog said the probe into four leading commercial banks and a state-run bank would focus on whether they followed regulations in offering huge loans to Hanbo Steel Co, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate.

Opposition parties, calling the loans the biggest financial scandal in the country's history, have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure creditor banks into offering loans to Hanbo without adequate collateral.
State prosecutors told reporters they had questioned six Hanbo officials on how the foundering steelmaker secured billions of dollars to finance a massive steel mill.
Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, filed for court receivership on Tuesday after piling up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) of loans from 61 banks and financial institutions.
The Office of Bank Supervision said the five banks under probe were Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank, SEOULBANK and the state-run Korea Development Bank.
"A team comprising seven investigators has been sent to each of the five banks," an office spokesman said.
"If a serious violation is found, severe punishment would be slapped on the banks and their management."

Credit rating company Standard & Poor said it placed Korea First Bank, which has the largest exposure to Hanbo with loans totalling 1.08 trillion won, on a watch list to reflect concerns over its deteriorating asset quality.
Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said more than 30 prosecutors sifted through Hanbo documents seized by police from offices of Hanbo Steel and its 15 affiliates on Tuesday.

"The special investigation of the Office of Bank Supervision will help our probe greatly," he said, adding prosecutors grilled three senior Hanbo executives responsible for the steelmaker's rapid expansion for the second day running.
He said he hoped the prosecution investigation would end within two weeks, although it could last longer.
President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a probe into the Hanbo case, which has put his anti-corruption drive on the line ahead of presidential elections in December.

After coming to power in 1993 on an anti-graft ticket, Kim promised to end legacies of the military-backed strongman rule of his predecessors by severing corrupt alliance betweeen politics and business.

Kim sent former presidents Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo to trial for taking huge sums from businessmen by rewarding them with soft loans and expensive projects. Chun is now serving a life sentence and Roh a 17-year jail term.
The Finance and Economy Ministry said the government would continue to pump cash into the money market to avoid a credit crunch and limit economic impact from Hanbo's debacle.
It said a further 2.0-2.5 trillion won would be released early next month after the central bank injected 3.6 trillion won since Friday.

The state Small and Medium Business Administration said on Wednesday more than 200 suppliers and subcontractors to Hanbo Steel had suffered from a financial squeeze due to a payment freeze by the steelmaker.

A local lumber shipping firm, Seyang Shipping Co, said it faced financial trouble because financial institutions avoided deals with the company whose chairman is a brother-in-law of Hanbo founder Chung Tae-soo.
